faq.a: Fructose metabolism depletes ATP, generating AMP which is degraded to uric acid.
faq.q: Why does fructose increase uric acid?

faq.a: In low‑resource settings, a typical clinical picture plus response to therapy may be sufficient, but crystals remain the gold standard.
faq.q: Can gout be diagnosed without crystal analysis?

faq.a: No; many patients remain asymptomatic, but they are at higher risk for gout and kidney disease.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man presents with sudden right great toe pain, swelling and redness. What is the next best step and why? — Perform joint aspiration to look for negatively birefringent crystals; confirms gout before starting therapy.

A patient with chronic kidney disease has serum uric acid 9 mg/dL but no joint symptoms. How would you manage? — Initiate lifestyle measures; start allopurinol only if uric acid remains >7 mg/dL or stones develop, because renal impairment limits excretion.

During malaria treatment, a patient develops flank pain and hematuria. Which metabolic disturbance should you suspect and what test confirms it? — Suspect uric acid nephrolithiasis from hemolysis‑induced hyperuricaemia; confirm with urine uric acid measurement and renal ultrasound.

Why is colchicine preferred over NSAIDs in a patient with severe anemia and CKD presenting with acute gout? — Colchicine has minimal renal excretion at low doses and does not affect platelet function, unlike NSAIDs which risk renal worsening and GI bleeding.

A patient on high‑dose thiazide diuretic develops gout. What medication adjustment would you make? — Switch to a potassium‑sparing diuretic or add a uricosuric; thiazides increase uric acid reabsorption via URAT1.

Explain why allopurinol should not be started during an acute gout flare without prophylaxis. — Initiating xanthine oxidase inhibition can shift purine metabolism, precipitating more crystal formation; start after flare resolves or give colchicine prophylaxis.

In a resource‑limited clinic, how would you differentiate gout from septic arthritis without advanced imaging? — Use clinical criteria (mono‑articular, rapid onset, tophi) and bedside joint aspiration with Gram stain; septic arthritis shows purulent fluid and organisms.

What lifestyle advice reduces uric acid production and why? — Limit purine‑rich foods, avoid fructose‑sweetened drinks, stay hydrated, and reduce alcohol; these measures lower substrate availability and improve renal clearance.
ai.title: Purine Metabolism and Clinical Implications
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Purine metabolism produces uric acid, whose accumulation causes gout and kidney stones. Understanding its pathways helps diagnose and manage hyperuricaemia, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Key end‑product: uric acid
Normal serum uric acid: 3.5–7.2 mg/dL (men), 2.4–6.0 mg/dL (women)
Hyperuricaemia predisposes to gout, nephrolithiasis and renal impairment
sections.p: Purines are nitrogenous bases that form DNA, RNA and energy molecules. Their breakdown ends with uric acid, which is eliminated by the kidneys.

b: Adenine → inosine → hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid
Guanine → guanosine → guanine → xanthine → uric acid
Xanthine oxidase is the rate‑limiting enzyme
sections.p: Purine nucleotides are de‑phosphorylated, de‑ribosylated and oxidised by xanthine oxidase to uric acid. The liver and intestine produce uric acid; kidneys excrete ~70 %.

b: High‑purine foods (organ meats, seafood) increase substrate
Fructose intake boosts ATP degradation → more uric acid
Renal impairment reduces excretion, raising serum levels
sections.p: Uric acid production is balanced by renal tubular reabsorption (via URAT1) and secretion (via GLUT9). Diet, cell turnover and drugs modify levels.

b: Overproduction: Lesch‑Nyhan, tumour lysis, high‑cell‑turnover infections (malaria, TB)
Under‑excretion: chronic kidney disease, diuretic use, dehydration
Genetic variants: URAT1 gain‑of‑function, GLUT9 loss‑of‑function
sections.p: Excess uric acid may be due to overproduction, under‑excretion, or both. Common tropical contributors include malaria‑induced hemolysis, HIV‑associated renal disease, and herbal remedies containing purines.

b: Acute gout: mono‑articular joint pain, swelling, erythema, often first MTP
Kidney stones: flank pain, hematuria, radiopaque on plain X‑ray
Chronic hyperuricaemia: asymptomatic but risk factor for CKD
sections.p: Hyperuricaemia manifests as gouty arthritis, uric acid nephrolithiasis, or chronic kidney disease. In low‑resource hospitals, bedside clues and simple tests guide diagnosis.
When laboratory tests are unavailable, use clinical criteria: recurrent mono‑articular attacks, typical joint distribution, and response to colchicine or allopurinol as presumptive diagnosis.

t.b: Is hyperuricaemia present? – Elevated >7.2 mg/dL (men) or >6.0 mg/dL (women) confirms excess uric acid
Is gout the cause of arthritis? – Needle‑shaped, negatively birefringent crystals under polarized light confirm gout
Are uric acid stones present? – Radiopaque stones on X‑ray or echogenic foci on ultrasound support nephrolithiasis
Is renal function impaired? – eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates reduced clearance of uric acid

b: Acute gout: colchicine, NSAIDs (if renal function allows), or corticosteroids
Chronic control: xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol, febuxostat) – chosen for efficacy; avoid in severe liver disease
Uricosurics (probenecid) – used when renal excretion is adequate; avoid in nephrolithiasis
Hydration: >2 L/day water to promote renal clearance
Diet: limit purine‑rich foods, fructose, and alcohol
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, lower uric acid production, and enhance excretion. Avoid drugs that increase uric acid (e.g., thiazides) when possible.

b: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) – rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals
Septic arthritis – purulent fluid, positive Gram stain
Calcium oxalate stones – radiopaque, different composition
sections.p: Conditions that mimic gout or uric acid stones.

b: Recent diuretic use can raise serum uric acid falsely
Acute illness may lower uric acid due to redistribution
Urine alkalinisation can dissolve uric acid crystals, giving false‑negative stone imaging
sections.p: Factors that may mask true uric acid status.

b: Distinguish gout from pseudogout by crystal shape and birefringence
Know first‑line acute gout therapy in renal impairment
Recall why allopurinol is contraindicated in acute gout flare without prophylaxis

whenToSeekHelp: Severe joint swelling with fever – possible septic arthritis
Acute renal colic with anuria – possible obstructing uric acid stone
Rapidly rising serum uric acid >12 mg/dL with renal failure – risk of tumor lysis syndrome
